newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: China presses Cambodia on flaring factory dispute.
newsitem.headline: China presses Cambodia on flaring factory dispute.

text.p: A delegation of Chinese officials is visiting Cambodia to discuss a disputed cement factory whose fate is again threatening to damage ties between Phnom Penh and Beijing.

The delegation, including about 10 officials from the government of Guangdong province and the Ministry of Coal Industry, wants the Cambodian government to reinstate a lease for a Chinese-built cement factory turned over to a Swiss firm in May, a Chinese embassy official told Reuters.

"They are still in negotiation with the Ministry of Industry, and they hope this project can be returned to the Chinese company," said the diplomat. "If not, the (Cambodian) government should compensate them."

The Chinese, the diplomat said, arrived earlier this week for a visit that coincided with Saturday's state visit of Swiss President Jean Pascal Delamuraz, but the embassy official said he did not know of any plans to meet Swiss officials.
"But they are ready to talk to the Swiss firm," he said.

The Chinese maintain that Guangdong Engineering Enterprises has invested $10 million in improving the Cambodia Cement Factory Ltd, which was donated to Cambodia the 1960s, only to have the government terminate their lease on the factory in May.
Guangdong officials, who were operating the factory in the southern province of Kampot, maintained the government acted improperly in awarding the plant contract to the Swiss Holderbank Group.
In a letter to Cambodian Foreign Minister Ung Huot in July, Cambodian Ambassador to China Khek Sysoda said Chinese diplomats were warning that the dispute could sour bilateral relations.

But business people said much of the dispute was rooted in a conflict between Guangdong and its former business partner, Cambodian Angkor Tranconimex, which maintains that most of the $10 million said to have been invested by the state-owned Chinese firm cannot be accounted for.
Suor Pheng, chairman of Angkor Tranconimex, said in July that it held the lease on the factory and had only brought in Guangdong to overhaul and manage the plant, forming a 50-50 venture.
His lease was terminated, he said, because the Chinese failed to perform as required and reached only 50 percent of production capacity.
The Holderbank Group is currently upgrading the factory through a local subsidiary, Naga Cement.
Periodic cement shortages have hit Cambodia's booming construction industry over recent months, and contractors have welcomed the increased local supply that Naga would bring.
